items.questionAndWhy: Does a performance incentive improve visual search by speeding every perceptual step or by changing how people explore a scene?
items.whatTheyDid: Shdeour and Yuval-Greenberg randomly assigned 40 students to a speed-contingent monetary lottery or control group in an eye-tracked Where's Waldo task; 37 were analyzed.
items.whatTheyFound: Correct searches averaged 15.93 seconds with reward versus 25.18 without. Accuracy and missed-trial differences were not significant. Rewarded participants made fewer fixations and revisited locations less often; mean fixation duration did not differ significantly. Decomposition favored more efficient exploration over uniformly faster processing.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX can test incentives in information-search exercises by measuring redundant sampling and target discovery separately from processing speed. The small student sample and laboratory task do not establish effects on intelligence analysis.
items.streamTitle: Reward changed visual search strategy more than processing speed
items.streamSummary: A randomized visual-search study found faster searches and fewer fixations under reward, without a significant accuracy difference. Strategy changes explained more of the advantage than faster within-fixation processing.
items.attribution: Shdeour and Yuval-Greenberg — Scientific Reports (randomized eye-tracking experiment; November 24, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Does the human language network share representations of meaning despite differences in grammar, sound and vocabulary?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers used multilingual-model representations to predict fMRI responses. One study included 24 speakers across 12 languages; another tested 27 speakers across nine additional languages using models trained on other language datasets.
items.whatTheyFound: Encoding models predicted responses within languages and generalized to unseen languages across language families and stimulus modalities. Removing meaning-related information reduced predictive fit. This is neural encoding evidence, not evidence that all cultures interpret a message identically.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX cross-language research can test semantic equivalence separately from surface linguistic form. Shared neural representation does not eliminate cultural differences in appraisal, values or behavioral responses.
items.streamTitle: Brain encoding models generalized meaning across 21 languages
items.streamSummary: Human fMRI encoding models generalized to unseen languages across 21 languages, supporting a shared semantic component. This does not demonstrate uniform cross-cultural interpretation or persuasion.
items.attribution: de Varda, Malik-Moraleda, Tuckute et al. — Nature Neuroscience (cross-language fMRI encoding study; November 23, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How does interpersonal incivility relate to team performance during high-pressure work, and does information seeking moderate the association?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers observed live trauma resuscitations in a hospital. Team-level analysis covered 52 teams; individual-level analysis covered 649 team-member observations across 59 resuscitations.
items.whatTheyFound: Each uncivil event was associated with a 3.53-minute delay to first X-ray. Exposure also related to greater patient pain; the association was weaker when professionals engaged in more information-seeking coping. Observational evidence cannot rule out crisis severity or other confounding.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX team-decision research, interpersonal friction and subsequent information seeking are observable candidate predictors of coordination delays. Test them in controlled training scenarios rather than importing the clinical effect size or asserting that information seeking causally offsets incivility.
items.streamTitle: Incivility correlated with delayed action in real crisis teams
items.streamSummary: Real trauma-team observations associated incivility with slower diagnostic action and patient pain; information seeking moderated one association. No causal intervention was tested.
items.attribution: Lim, Goh, Tay et al. — Scientific Reports (naturalistic crisis-team field study; November 24, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can civilian organizations and armed forces prepare jointly to sustain essential services during crises?
items.whatTheyDid: At the November 24 NATO Resilience Symposium in Rome, more than 300 representatives from government, military, industry, academia and other organizations discussed civil-military resilience. NATO announced guidance for joint preparation, planning and exercises.
items.whatTheyFound: The official account establishes a new guidance initiative and a whole-of-society coordination objective. It does not provide an outcome evaluation or demonstrate improved readiness.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX exercises could assess shared situational understanding, coordination delays and conflicting civilian-military service priorities under simulated disruption. The value of the guidance requires evaluation rather than inference from its issuance.
items.streamTitle: NATO issued public-private resilience cooperation guidance
items.streamSummary: NATO announced public-private resilience guidance on November 24, emphasizing joint planning and exercises to sustain essential services. Readiness gains were not measured.

items.questionAndWhy: Do rating-scale design choices affect automated AI evaluations even when the object being judged remains the same?
items.whatTheyDid: Kim and colleagues systematically varied scale width, granularity, offset, symmetry and boundaries across zero-shot LLM-judge models and benchmarks.
items.whatTheyFound: Score distributions, calibration and robustness changed with scale design, especially on judgment-heavy tasks. Shifted and narrow scales often produced large deviations. Stronger judges were generally more robust. The preprint concerns benchmark scoring, not human judgments or universal model performance.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX automated rubric evaluations should freeze and version scales, then test score stability under equivalent rescalings before comparing research outputs across runs. Human expert agreement still needs independent testing.
items.streamTitle: Changing numerical rating scales shifted AI judge scores
items.streamSummary: An LLM-judge benchmark found scale width and placement changed scores and calibration even without changing the evaluated content. Larger judges were generally more robust.
items.attribution: Kim, Kim, Kum, Song and Park — arXiv preprint (November 19, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: When several study designs address the same causal question, what does agreement or disagreement between estimates actually establish?
items.whatTheyDid: García Meixide and Ríos Insua formalized identification multiplicity using causal targets, shared assumptions and dependence among estimates. Fourteen examples span adjustment, panel comparisons, instruments, mediators, discontinuities and other designs.
items.whatTheyFound: Their theoretical decomposition shows that differences may reflect distinct estimands or failures of identification assumptions. Agreement cannot detect biases common to all approaches. Combining estimates requires a defensible common target or explicitly stated alternative interpretation; weighting alone is insufficient.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX nonrandomized intervention assessment can maintain an estimand-and-assumption ledger before comparing effect estimates from different evidence sources. Agreement across analyses sharing the same confounding risk should not count as independent corroboration. This is methodological theory, not a validated behavioral forecast.
items.streamTitle: Causal triangulation framework separated target differences from assumption failures
items.streamSummary: A formal triangulation framework distinguishes differences in causal targets from identification discrepancies and explains why agreement cannot eliminate shared bias.
items.attribution: García Meixide and Ríos Insua — arXiv preprint (causal identification methodology; November 23, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can causal response curves differ across subgroups when exposure varies continuously rather than being simply present or absent?
items.whatTheyDid: Bargagli-Stoffi and colleagues combined doubly robust curve estimation with recursive partitioning, constructing subgroup-specific pseudo-outcomes. They derived convergence conditions and illustrated the method using US county pollution and mortality data from 2000–2019.
items.whatTheyFound: The formal results show why a conventional continuous-treatment pseudo-outcome is inadequate for this subgroup-search objective. The algorithm identifies differences in curve shapes under its assumptions and is implemented in the R package discoverHTE. The application is environmental, not behavioral.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX could test whether intervention intensity has different response curves in consented behavioral studies rather than assuming one linear effect or a binary exposure. Transfer is untested and requires credible confounding control, exposure overlap and independent subgroup validation.
items.streamTitle: Interpretable subgroup discovery extended causal modeling to continuous treatment doses
items.streamSummary: A new recursive partitioning method discovers heterogeneous causal dose-response curves with subgroup-specific estimation. Behavioral applications remain untested.
items.attribution: Bargagli-Stoffi, Pham, Kennedy et al. — arXiv preprint (causal estimation methods; November 23, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can researchers capture temporally aligned physiological and visual-attention data during ordinary smartphone interactions?
items.whatTheyDid: Mishra and colleagues recorded 30 participants using their most-used smartphone application for ten minutes, then viewing a nature video for five minutes. They collected 64-channel EEG, wearable eye tracking, photoplethysmography, skin conductance and questionnaires.
items.whatTheyFound: The open BIDS-format dataset uses hardware trigger synchronization and is available on OpenNeuro as ds007537. It provides measurement infrastructure; the fixed sequence and differing activities do not establish causal effects of smartphone use or identify particular emotional states.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX can examine this dataset and synchronization protocol when designing consented studies of attention during digital media use. Physiological signals need independent validation against specific cognitive and behavioral outcomes; they do not directly reveal belief or persuasion.
items.streamTitle: Synchronized smartphone-use dataset combines gaze and physiological signals
items.streamSummary: A public dataset aligns EEG, gaze and physiological recordings during smartphone use in 30 people. It enables multimodal attention research, not causal conclusions about media effects.
items.attribution: Mishra, Gandhi and Gandhi — Scientific Data (data descriptor; November 11, 2026)
